title: Eigenvectors and eigenvalues: invariant directions and diagonalization
summary: 3Blue1Brown’s Essence of Linear Algebra Chapter 14 visually introduces eigenvectors and eigenvalues as the invariant directions of a linear transformation. The video works through a concrete 2D example where the transformation stretches along specific lines (the x-axis and a diagonal line), then formalizes the eigenvector equation Av = λv, leading to the standard determinant-based eigenvalue computation det(A − λI) = 0. It shows how to extract eigenvectors by solving (A − λI)v = 0, gives concrete eigenvectors for the example (e.g., along (1,0) and (−1,1)), and discusses special cases such as rotations (which may have no real eigenvectors) and shear (limited eigenvectors). The concept of an eigenbasis is introduced, explaining how if a matrix has enough eigenvectors, changing to that basis diagonalizes the transformation, making computations such as high powers of A straightforward. The video also connects these ideas to change of basis and emphasizes when diagonalization is beneficial (and when it isn’t).

sections.title: Intuition: eigenvectors and invariant directions
sections.description: Introduction to eigenvectors as directions that stay on their span under a linear transformation and the role of spans of basis vectors in understanding a matrix.

sections.title: Concrete 2D example: matrix with columns (3,0) and (1,2)
sections.description: Demonstrates a 2D transformation where i-hat is stretched along the x-axis (eigenvalue 3) and a diagonal eigenvector along (-1,1) with eigenvalue 2.

sections.title: Formal eigenvector equation Av = λv
sections.description: Presents the eigenvector equation and reframes it as a homogeneous system via (A − λI)v = 0.

sections.title: Eigenvalues via determinant: det(A − λI) = 0
sections.description: Shows how to compute eigenvalues by solving det(A − λI) = 0; for the example A = [[3,1],[0,2]] the eigenvalues are 2 and 3.

sections.title: Eigenvectors for specific eigenvalues
sections.description: Solves for eigenvectors: λ=2 yields vectors along (−1,1); λ=3 yields vectors along (1,0); illustrates invariant directions.

sections.title: Other examples: rotation and shear
sections.description: Discusses a 2D rotation (no real eigenvectors; eigenvalues ±i) and a shear (fixed x-axis, eigenvectors with eigenvalue 1 along x-axis).

sections.title: Eigenbasis and diagonalization
sections.description: If a full set of eigenvectors exists, they form an eigenbasis; the transformation is diagonal in that basis, with eigenvalues on the diagonal.

sections.title: Power and change of basis reminder
sections.description: Notes that diagonalization makes computing powers easier (e.g., A^n = P D^n P^{-1}); mentions change-of-basis concepts.

featured_techniques.technique: Deriving eigenvalues via det(A − λI) = 0 (characteristic equation)
Using eigenbasis to compute powers (A^n) easily
